title: Ang 634–641: Sorath ashtpadis
tomorrow: why would a hymn about God bring up your teeth?

segments.voice: Last time, unmoved: Guru Tegh Bahadur's portrait of someone who feels pain and praise and isn't ruled by either. A new week, and the hymns get longer.

It's past midnight at the dholki, four nights before the wedding. The aunties have been singing for an hour, one verse handing off to the next, the drum never stopping, and somebody's cousin finally asks why the song needs so many verses to say one thing. Nobody answers. They just start the next one. On ang 634, Guru Nanak does the same. Sorath's ashtpadis begin: longer hymns, built of many stanzas, circling one thought until it lands.
screen: `PAST MIDNIGHT AT THE DHOLKI.` → `WHY SO MANY VERSES?` → `CIRCLING ONE THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: So what's the one thought? Here's the first ashtpadi, in paraphrase. I don't fall into two-mindedness. I worship no one but the Lord. I don't go wandering to tombs and cremation grounds. Caught by craving, I don't slip into other people's houses. The Name has quenched my thirst. Listen to the shape of it. Each line names a door, and walks past it. Not this. Not that. Not there either. A short hymn would tell you the destination. This one takes you down the hallway, door after door, until you feel why none of them is the one. That's what the length is for. By the time the stanzas reach the Name, you've already walked past everything else with him. The thirst that sent you to all those doors is the thing that's finally quenched. And that's why the aunties keep singing. A long song isn't saying more. It's staying longer, until the one thing is in your body, not just your ears. On the page, longer hymns like these carry their own heading, ashtpadi, so a reader knows to settle in.
screen: `THE ONE THOUGHT: NO OTHER DOOR.` · `NOT THIS, NOT THAT, NOT THERE.` · `THE NAME QUENCHES THE THIRST.` · `A LONG SONG STAYS LONGER.` · then, large: `LONGER HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Choose one steady sound near you: a fan, traffic, rain, a song playing low. Listen only to that sound for the whole sit. When your attention drifts to another door, notice it, and walk back to the one sound.
Ang 634. Where Sorath's ashtpadis begin: Guru Nanak's longer hymn that walks past every door to the Name.
Your line: longer hymns, staying until the one thing lands. The drum is still going. See you tomorrow.
